passage:
Rajni: Meera hasn't answered in five months. not one reply
Vishal: I know. Have you thought about why?
Rajni: I keep going back to the day I told my daughter in front of everyone that marrying him was a mistake. And the times I read her diary. I never said sorry
Vishal: Will you write to her?
Rajni: One letter. Only an apology. I won't ask her to come home. And I won't call her friends or the aunts any more. I did last year and I think it pushed her further
Vishal: That sounds right. Will you explain yourself in it?
Rajni: No. She decides what happens next
Vishal: I'll sit with you when you write it
Rajni: Thank you. It hurts. But I'd rather she comes back slowly than never

qa.q: How long has Meera not replied?
qa.a: Meera has not replied for five months.

qa.q: What does Rajni feel about the public remark and the diary?
qa.a: Rajni feels regret and sees these as hurtful acts, for which Rajni never apologised.

qa.q: What is Rajni's plan for the letter?
qa.a: One letter with only an apology, without asking Meera to come home and without explaining or defending.

qa.q: How might Meera have felt about the earlier calls to her friends and the aunts?
qa.a: Pressured and pushed further away, as Rajni suspects.

grounding: A parent whose child has cut contact feels hurt, plans an apology without defending, stops pressuring through relatives, and lets the child decide.

passage:
Mehak, you ask why I don't push your uncle Harpreet to come to the family functions. Let your Amandeep bua tell you.

When I was twenty-five, my younger brother stopped speaking to me. No reason I could see. I was bewildered, and so hurt. I asked my mother, my cousins, even his friends, to tell him to call me. That only made it worse.

Then my cousin brought me a letter from him. It said that when our father died, I had taken over everything, the house, the decisions, even his wedding, and never once asked what he wanted. Reading it, I wanted to defend every choice.

That was my turning point. I didn't defend. I wrote back: "You're right. I took over. I'm sorry. I won't send anyone to you again. Whenever you're ready, I'm here."

Then I waited. Three years. One Lohri he came to the door with rewri. We talk now. Slowly.

qa.q: How long did Amandeep wait after writing back?
How did young Amandeep feel when her brother stopped speaking to her?
qa.a: She felt bewildered and deeply hurt, not understanding why.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Amandeep's story?
qa.a: Reading her brother's letter and choosing not to defend herself, she apologised, stopped sending relatives, and let him return at his own pace.

qa.q: How might Amandeep's brother have felt when relatives kept pressing him to call?
qa.a: He likely felt pressured and unheard, which made him pull further away.

grounding: An elder's story shows a young woman whose brother cut her off, who stopped defending herself, apologised, stopped pressuring him through relatives and let him return at his own pace.

passage:
Ayesha's wedding was in three weeks, and Tarun still hadn't been invited. His younger sister had stopped answering his calls eight months ago, after a family dinner that ended in shouting. He didn't even fully know why.

His mother kept saying, "I'll talk to her." His aunt kept saying, "I'll make her call you." Nothing worked. The deadline made it worse; every day, Tarun felt more bewildered and more hurt.

Then his cousin said quietly, "She says you never listen. That you always decide what's right for her."

Tarun wanted to argue. He had only ever been trying to help! He stopped himself.

That night he asked his mother and aunt to stop pushing her. Then he wrote Ayesha a short message: "I'm sorry for how I've treated your choices. I didn't listen. I won't send anyone to you again. I'd love to be at your wedding, but only if you want me there."

Two weeks later, a card arrived. Inside, one line: "Come."

qa.q: How long ago had Ayesha stopped answering Tarun's calls?
qa.a: She stopped answering eight months ago.

qa.q: How did Tarun feel as the wedding came closer without an invitation?
qa.a: Tarun felt more bewildered and hurt every day.

qa.q: What did Tarun do that finally helped?
qa.a: He stopped relatives from pressuring Ayesha, apologised without defending himself, and left the choice to come back to her.

qa.q: How might Ayesha have felt receiving Tarun's message?
qa.a: Ayesha may have felt heard and less pressured, which gave her room to invite him.

grounding: The story shows a young man whose sister cut him off, who listens instead of defending, apologises, stops pressuring her through relatives and lets her choose.
